meta.headline: **Partial implementation (B)** is the dominant outcome (143 of 252 recommendations), and Tanzania gives a detailed National Report on socio-economic and service measures: health financing (TZS 1.31 to 3.104 trillion), school construction and a Re-Entry Guideline for pregnant girls, the Second National Plan of Action on violence against women and children (2024/25-2028/29), a National Action Plan on persons with albinism, the Mama Samia legal aid campaign and amendments to the Media Services Act and related laws. **Fully implemented (A)** are the ban on expelling pregnant schoolgirls, birth registration, older persons, climate participation and rural communication infrastructure. **No relevant action (C)** persists on ratifying the Convention against Torture and other treaties, the death penalty (a de facto moratorium only), child marriage (the Law of Marriage Act is still only under consultation), decriminalisation of same-sex relations, corporal punishment and the second National Human Rights Action Plan. **Contrary measures (E)** apply to 14 recommendations on freedom of expression, assembly, political participation and indigenous peoples: the nationwide internet shutdown after the 29 October 2025 elections, the shutdown of more than 80,000 websites (May 2025), reported lethal force, arrests and enforced disappearances (which the State rejects), disqualification of opposition candidates and the position that no group is indigenous.

recommendations.text: Respect the right to confidentiality and dignity of LGBTI+ persons by banning invasive and demeaning procedures disguised as evidence-gathering, such as anal examinations

blocks.summary: Abolish the death penalty or adopt a formal moratorium
blocks.rationale: Tanzania maintains a de facto moratorium (no execution since 1994) but the mandatory death penalty remains in the Penal Code and no formal moratorium or awareness campaign has followed.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 64 — United Republic of Tanzania: "The URT maintained its de facto moratorium on the death penalty, and no executions have been carried out since 1994"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 11 — JS28: "the mandatory death penalty for the murder and treason as prescribed in the Penal Code required reform"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 9 — United Nations country team: "expressed concern about the lack of implementation of those commitments"

recommendations.text: Establish an immediate formal moratorium on the mandatory death penalty with a view to its abolition and ratify the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty
Abolish the death penalty and ratify the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty
Adopt a de jure moratorium on capital executions and ratify the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty
Abolish the death penalty in all circumstances
Fully abolish the death penalty in all circumstances and ratify the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty
Abolish the death penalty and commute all death sentences to alternative sentences
Adopt a formal moratorium on executions with a view to abolishing the death penalty

blocks.summary: Awareness campaigns and public debates on the death penalty
blocks.rationale: The UN country team expresses concern about the lack of implementation of this commitment.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 9 — United Nations country team: "expressed concern about the lack of implementation of those commitments"

recommendations.text: Strengthen awareness-raising campaigns on the death penalty and hold public debates on the subject from a human rights perspective, including in parliament, with a view to realizing its definitive abolition and the ratification of the Second Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, aiming at the abolition of the death penalty, as soon as possible

blocks.summary: Establish a moratorium on executions
blocks.rationale: Tanzania maintains a de facto moratorium (no execution since 1994) which it has not formalised.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 64 — United Republic of Tanzania: "The URT maintained its de facto moratorium on the death penalty, and no executions have been carried out since 1994"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 11 — JS28: "As no executions had been carried out since 1994, a de facto moratorium appeared to be in place"

recommendations.text: Establish a moratorium on executions with a view to abolishing the death penalty

blocks.summary: Prevent child labour and sexual abuse of children
blocks.rationale: A National Action Plan on the Elimination of Child Labour (2025/26-2029/30) was adopted and child labour fell from 33.8% to 25.4%; JS10 reports it remains widespread.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 32 — United Republic of Tanzania: "These interventions contributed to reducing child labour from 33.8% to 25.4% in 2024"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 41 — JS10: "child labour had remained widespread, particularly in agriculture, fishing, mining, and domestic work"

recommendations.text: Intensify the work done to prevent and investigate cases of sexual abuse of children and eliminate the practice of female genital mutilation
Continue its efforts to curtail child labour
Continue its efforts, including existing programmes, to eliminate child labour in the country
Continue the efforts undertaken to eliminate child labour
Continue to enhance efforts to prevent child labour

blocks.summary: Improve access to adequate housing, water and sanitation
blocks.rationale: Housing construction loans reached 31% of loans (TZS 659.3 billion) and the Zanzibar Housing Corporation built 144 units; UNCT finds partial implementation.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 89 — United Republic of Tanzania: "accessible housing construction loans, which reached 31% of loans worth TZS 659.3 billion"

recommendations.text: Improve access to adequate housing, safe drinking water and adequate sanitation

blocks.summary: Reduce poverty, including among persons with albinism
blocks.rationale: National poverty fell from 26.4% (2020) to 24.9% (2025), TASAF reached 1.36 million households and interest-free loans were extended to persons with disabilities including albinism.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 66 — United Republic of Tanzania: "national basic needs poverty rate declined from 26.4% in 2020 to 24.9% in 2025"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 85 — United Republic of Tanzania: "TASAF benefited a total of 1.36 million households with 5,195,605 beneficiaries"

recommendations.text: Continue efforts to reduce poverty, especially by enhancing access to quality education and skills development, as well as by improving conditions for farmers, small businesses and investors to thrive
Ensure that persons with albinism benefit from programmes to combat poverty, in particular through special measures
Ensure that persons with albinism are covered by anti-poverty programmes

blocks.summary: Improve drinking water and sanitation in rural areas
blocks.rationale: WSDP III completed 1,373 rural projects and raised rural access to 85.2%; UNCT notes disparities in rural and informal settlements.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 91 — United Republic of Tanzania: "increased access to water in rural areas to 85.2%, and 92.5 % in urban areas"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 29 — United Nations country team: "disparities in access to water in rural and informal settlements"

recommendations.text: Continue to take necessary measures to improve the provision of clean drinking water and sanitation facilities to rural areas
Redouble efforts to resolve the disparity in accessing water services in urban and rural areas

themes.theme: Prohibition of torture & ill-treatment (including cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment)

blocks.summary: Strengthen the fight against torture and ill-treatment; prohibit corporal punishment
blocks.rationale: The UN country team finds the torture recommendation not implemented, JS15 reports ongoing risks in police custody and corporal punishment remains lawful.
evidence: Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 13 — JS15: "ongoing risks of torture and ill-treatment in police custody"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 70 — JS10: "corporal punishment remained lawful and widely practices in homes and schools"

recommendations.text: Strengthen the fight against torture and ill-treatment

blocks.summary: Prohibit corporal punishment
blocks.rationale: Corporal punishment remains lawful in schools and homes.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 49 — UNESCO: "recommended legally proscribing corporal punishment in education settings"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 70 — JS10: "corporal punishment remained lawful and widely practices in homes and schools"

recommendations.text: Prohibit all forms of corporal punishment

blocks.summary: Investigate arbitrary arrest and detention of political opponents and activists
blocks.rationale: A Presidential Commission of Inquiry (November 2025) and a Criminal Investigation Commission (May 2026) were set up on the post-election unrest; the State rejects allegations of arbitrary arrests.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 7 — United Republic of Tanzania: "a Presidential Commission of Inquiry was established on 18 November, 2025 to examine the unrest that occurred during and after the General Elections"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 11 — United Republic of Tanzania: "It rejected the allegations of widespread arbitrary arrests and detentions"

recommendations.text: Take steps to promptly and effectively investigate and provide information on cases of arbitrary arrest and detention of political opponents, activists, protesters and dissenting journalists

blocks.summary: Investigate arbitrary arrests and ensure fair hearings
blocks.rationale: Decision to Charge Guidelines (2023) and DPP Guidelines No. 2 of 2024 strengthened prosecutorial safeguards, and a Commission of Inquiry on the post-election unrest was created; special procedures report arbitrary arrests of protesters and opposition leaders.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 48 — United Republic of Tanzania: "The Decision to Charge Guidelines (2023) and Director of Public Prosecutions Guidelines No. 2 of 2024 strengthened investigation standards"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 16 — United Nations country team: "arrests of an opposition leader during a public rally and of several young people in the aftermath of the October 2025 elections"

recommendations.text: Ensure fair and public hearings for those criminally charged and to prevent arbitrary arrests

blocks.summary: Re-entry to education for pregnant girls and young mothers
blocks.rationale: Education Circular No. 2 of 2021 and a Re-Entry Guideline (2022) allow return after childbirth (13,272 returned); JS2 notes restrictive provisions, discretion of schools and no measure against pregnancy tests.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 104 — United Republic of Tanzania: "the Re-Entry Guideline of 2022, which enabled 13,272 students to return to school"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 59 — JS2: "existing laws and policies neither adequately addressed, nor sufficiently facilitated, their re-entry into the education system"

recommendations.text: Strengthen measures to safeguard the health rights of women, particularly on issues relating to prenatal and postnatal care of pregnant women

blocks.summary: Amend laws restricting freedom of expression, assembly and association
blocks.rationale: The Media Services, Access to Information, Cybercrimes, Political Parties, Statistics and Electronic and Postal Communications Acts were amended (R.E. 2023), removing criminal defamation provisions, and the political-rally ban was lifted (2022-2023); stakeholders consider that licensing and content restrictions remain.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 51 — United Republic of Tanzania: "These reforms removed criminal defamation provisions and strengthened safeguards for editorial independence, professional standards, and responsible media practice"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 4 — United Republic of Tanzania: "Its recommendations led to lifting the ban on political party rallies"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 29 — JS3: "licensing requirements and content restrictions"

recommendations.text: Amend or repeal aspects of the Political Parties Act, the Media Services Act and the Electronic and Postal Communications Act to promote freedom of expression

blocks.summary: Amend the NGO regulations in line with international standards
blocks.rationale: JS5 and JS21 report broad registration discretion and burdensome compliance; 14 LGBTI-serving organisations were deregistered.
evidence: Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 32 — JS5: "granted the Authorities broad discretion to deny registration or impose restrictions on organizations"

recommendations.text: Amend the Non-Governmental Organizations Act (Amendments) Regulation 2018 in line with international human rights standards on freedoms of association and peaceful assembly

blocks.summary: Ensure freedom of assembly and a safe environment for parties, media and civil society
blocks.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
blocks.rationale: Special procedures and stakeholders report restriction of opposition rallies, disqualification of opposition candidates, the October 2025 internet shutdown and arrests; the State rejects the allegations.
evidence: Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 36 — JS21: "the Authorities had systematically restricted opposition rallies and had curtailed the movement of members of opposition parties"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 23 — Special procedure mandate holders: "had reportedly resulted in the disqualification of opposition candidates during the nomination process"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 20 — United Republic of Tanzania: "the Internet disruption following the events of 29 October 2025 had been a temporary measure"

recommendations.text: Respect fully and protect the rights to freedom of assembly and freedom of expression, and enshrine into law the right to a safe and enabling environment for human rights defenders, journalists and media workers

Ensure freedom of assembly and expression to enable a political and civic space, so that political parties, the media and civil society organizations can operate safely and fully exercise their rights

Create and maintain a safe and conducive environment where all political parties and civil society organizations can exercise their rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of political participation without fear of reprisal

blocks.summary: Amend laws restricting freedom of expression, assembly and association
blocks.rationale: The Media Services, Access to Information, Cybercrimes, Political Parties, Statistics and Electronic and Postal Communications Acts were amended (R.E. 2023), removing criminal defamation provisions, and the political-rally ban was lifted (2022-2023); stakeholders consider that licensing and content restrictions remain.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the laws governing the right to freedom of peaceful assembly are fully in line with the provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights

Guarantee freedom of assembly, association, expression and press freedom for members of all political parties, the media and civil society organizations by, inter alia, reforming the Cybercrimes Act and the Media Act

blocks.summary: Amend the Law of Marriage Act and raise the minimum age of marriage to 18
blocks.rationale: Amendment is only 'under consultation'; the High Court ordered it in 2016 and JS2 notes the Act still allows girls to marry at 14.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 26 — United Republic of Tanzania: "Amendment of the Law of Marriage Act, Cap. 29, are under consultation as part of broader legal reforms"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 69 — JS2: "the Law of Marriage Act, which allowed girls as young as 14 years of age to marry, had not been amended"

recommendations.text: Amend the 1971 Law of Marriage Act to raise the marriage age for girls to 18 years, as ordered by the Supreme Court of Appeal in 2019
Revise the Law of Marriage Act of 1971 to establish the minimum age of marriage at 18 years for both girls and boys with a view to ending child, early and forced marriages
Revise the 1971 Law of Marriage Act to set the minimum age of marriage to 18 years for both girls and boys
Amend the Law of Marriage Act (1971) and other legislation to reflect the Court of Appeals decision on the minimum age of marriage
Complete the reforms necessary to raise the minimum legal age of marriage for boys and girls to 18 years and sensitize people of the importance of protecting the rights of all children
Harmonize the regulations regarding the minimum age of marriage and prohibit early and child marriages and unions
Take urgent steps to amend legislation to outlaw all forms of child marriage, safeguard women’s rights to sexual and reproductive health and end violence against women and children
Amend the Law of Marriage Act from 1971 to set the minimum age of marriage at 18 years for both boys and girls
Continue to combat the phenomena of child, early and forced marriage by amending the relevant legislation accordingly

blocks.summary: Protect children's rights
blocks.rationale: Child helpline, online-protection campaign, child justice strategy, child labour action plan and fee-free basic education were implemented; legislation on marriage and corporal punishment is unchanged.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 30 — United Republic of Tanzania: "National Child Online Protection Campaign in all 26 regions of Mainland Tanzania"

recommendations.text: Continue to protect the rights of children through the strengthening of protective policies and legislation, in particular by meeting their educational needs and by sanctioning violations of their rights

blocks.summary: Prohibit corporal punishment
blocks.rationale: Corporal punishment remains lawful in schools and homes.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 49 — UNESCO: "recommended legally proscribing corporal punishment in education settings"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 70 — JS10: "corporal punishment remained lawful and widely practices in homes and schools"

recommendations.text: Protect children’s rights to access to health and education by abolishing corporal punishment in schools

themes.theme: Right to participate in public affairs & right to vote

blocks.summary: Electoral reform and election observation
blocks.rationale: Electoral laws were amended (2024), 164 CSOs were accredited for voter education and 12 international observer missions attended the 2025 elections; SADC found the elections fell short of its principles and special procedures raised questions on the electoral commission's independence.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 62 — United Republic of Tanzania: "12 international observer missions comprising 135 observers observed the elections"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 35 — JS7: "found that the elections had fallen short of its principles and guidelines"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 21 — United Nations country team: "expressed concern about the independence and impartiality of the Independent National Electoral Commission"

recommendations.text: Promote citizens’ ability to choose their government in free and fair periodic elections by reforming election observation and voter education programmes and by preventing political violence

Enable future free, fair and transparent elections by undertaking political and electoral reforms, including the implementation of the recommendations issued in the final report of the European Union election observation mission to the United Republic of Tanzania of 2015

blocks.summary: Ensure a safe and enabling environment for political parties, civil society and defenders
blocks.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
blocks.rationale: Opposition rallies were restricted, opposition candidates disqualified and the 29 October 2025 elections followed by an internet shutdown and reports of lethal force; the State rejects the allegations.
evidence: Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 36 — JS21: "the Authorities had systematically restricted opposition rallies and had curtailed the movement of members of opposition parties"
UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 23 — Special procedure mandate holders: "had reportedly resulted in the disqualification of opposition candidates during the nomination process"

recommendations.text: Ensure a safe and enabling environment for political parties, civil society organizations and human rights defenders to exercise their legitimate activities effectively and independently

blocks.summary: Accessibility of public places and transport
blocks.rationale: New courts, health facilities and schools incorporate ramps and accessible toilets, and accessibility regulations for public transport apply.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 40 — United Republic of Tanzania: "newly constructed courts, Integrated Justice Centres, health facilities, schools and other public buildings incorporated ramps, accessible toilets and other universal accessibility features"

recommendations.text: Improve accessibility of persons with disabilities to public places, including public buildings and public transport services

blocks.summary: Protect the rights of women, children and persons with disabilities
blocks.rationale: Gender, child-protection and disability policies were adopted and expanded.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 23 — United Republic of Tanzania: "the National Gender and Women Development Policy of 2023"

recommendations.text: Sustain efforts and commitments in protecting the rights of women, children and people with disabilities

themes.theme: Persons with disabilities: definition, general principles

blocks.summary: Empower persons with disabilities
blocks.rationale: The Persons with Disabilities Policy was revised (2023), a National Assistive Technology Strategy 2024-2027 launched and interest-free loans extended; UNCT finds partial implementation.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 34 — United Republic of Tanzania: "the Person with Disabilities Policy of 2004 was revised in 2023"
National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 35 — United Republic of Tanzania: "launched the National Assistive Technology Strategy (2024-2027) on 3rd December, 2024"

recommendations.text: Continue to implement national policies and programmes aimed at empowering persons with disabilities (Syrian Arab Republic).

blocks.summary: Combat child marriage, FGM and discrimination against women
blocks.rationale: FGM prevalence fell from 10% to about 5% under national strategies, marriage registration was digitalised through RITA and pregnant girls may return to school; the Law of Marriage Act has not been amended.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 55 — United Republic of Tanzania: "adopted the National Multisectoral Strategy to End Female Genital Mutilation (2025/26–2029/30)"

National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 26 — United Republic of Tanzania: "continued strengthening of the civil registration system, including marriage registration services administered by RITA"

recommendations.text: Strengthen the policies and the legal framework to ensure marriage registration to address cases of early child marriage

blocks.summary: Clarify land rights and safeguard indigenous culture and livelihoods
blocks.meaning: Information or measures taken are contrary to, or reflect rejection of, the recommendation
blocks.rationale: Tanzania states that no group is recognised as indigenous; special procedures and stakeholders report forced evictions in Ngorongoro and Ruaha.
evidence: UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 54 — United Republic of Tanzania: "no special group or community in the country was recognized as indigenous"
Stakeholders' Summary (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/3), para. 76 — JS18: "planned eviction of pastoralists from at least 25 villages in Ngorongoro Division"

recommendations.text: Clarify land rights and safeguard indigenous culture, including traditional livelihoods, especially for indigenous peoples, and adopt positive measures to protect them

blocks.summary: Protect refugee claimants and ensure voluntary repatriation
blocks.rationale: Tanzania hosts 164,901 refugees with UNHCR; the UN country team recommendations that non-refoulement be respected in the Burundi tripartite repatriation.
evidence: National Report (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/1), para. 63 — United Republic of Tanzania: "Tanzania hosted 164,901 refugees in partnership with UNHCR and their country of origin"

UN Compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/53/TZA/2), para. 56 — United Nations country team: "comply with the principle of non-refoulement in the implementation of the tripartite agreement on the repatriation of Burundian refugees"

recommendations.text: Uphold the rights of refugee claimants in the United Republic of Tanzania and ensure that those seeking asylum are protected pending status determination, that refugee status is determined in an impartial, fair and timely manner and that any repatriation of refugee claimants is conducted in accordance with the international human rights obligations of the United Republic of Tanzania (Canada).
